The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

derivations.claim:
Put $c=2\pi\epsilon>0$ and define $D_cg(\xi)=c^{-d/2}g(\xi/c)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$. A null set is sent to a null set by the same change-of-variables theorem [F2], so this definition is independent of the representative of $g$. Apply [F2] to $T(\eta)=c\eta$, whose Jacobian determinant is $c^d$, and to the nonnegative function $f(\xi)=|g(\xi/c)|^2$. This gives
$$ \|D_cg\|_2^2=c^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(\xi/c)|^2\,d\xi =c^{-d}c^d\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(\eta)|^2\,d\eta =\|g\|_2^2. $$
The inverse is $D_{1/c}$, as direct substitution shows, so $D_c$ is unitary.

By [F3], $\mathcal F_\epsilon u=D_c\mathcal F_2u$ for every $u\in\mathcal S$. Both factors extend unitarily by step 1.1 and [F1], so their composition is a unitary extension to $L^2$. If $G$ were another continuous extension, then $D_c^{-1}G$ would be a continuous extension of $\mathcal F_2$; uniqueness in [F1] gives $D_c^{-1}G=\mathcal F_2$, hence $G=D_c\mathcal F_2$.

Choose a measurable representative of the class $u\in L^2$ and let $g(x,y)=K_\epsilon(x,y)u(y)$, which is product-measurable. otin N$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] in $L^2$ gives $\int|g(x,y)|\,dy\leq\|K_\epsilon(x,\cdot)\|_2\|u\|_2<\infty$, so all four section integrals are finite and their signed combination is $\int K_\epsilon(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. Define $A_\epsilon u(x)$ by that integral for $x
otin N$ and by $0$ for $x\in N$; the positive/negative-part representation shows this is measurable. If the representative of $u$ is changed on a null set, each good section integral is unchanged, so this defines the same $L^2$ class. For $x
otin N$, the same Cauchy–Schwarz estimate [F6] gives $$ |A_\epsilon u(x)|^2\leq\left(\int|K_\epsilon(x,y)|^2\,dyight)\|u\|_2^2. $$ Integrating in $x$ and using [F3] shows $A_\epsilon u\in L^2$ and $\|A_\epsilon u\|_2\leq\|K_\epsilon\|_2\|u\|_2$. derivations.claim: For $Z=(q,p)$, define the normalized Gaussian packet $$ g_Z^\epsilon(x):=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{-|x-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}e^{ip\cdot(x-q/2)/\epsilon}. $$ Its norm is $1$ by [F3] at zero after applying [F9] to the translation and positive scaling of the nonnegative Gaussian. For $u\in\mathcal S$, put $V_\epsilon u(Z)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle$. The Fourier transform of the shifted Gaussian gives $$ \langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}(2\pi\epsilon)^{d/2}\mathcal F_\epsilon\!\left(u(\,\cdot\,)e^{-|\cdot-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}\right)(p). $$ Plancherel [F2], followed by Tonelli [F4] and the Gaussian integral from [F3] after [F9], gives $$ \|V_\epsilon u\|_2^2=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int|\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle|^2\,dq\,dp=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int\!\!\int |u(x)|^2e^{-|x-q|^2/\epsilon}\,dx\,dq=\|u\|_2^2. $$ The middle equality follows from Plancherel [F2] for each fixed $q$; the final equality uses the Gaussian integral [F3] in $q$, with Tonelli [F4]. The same identity holds for all $u\in L^2$ by [F2] and Tonelli [F4]. Polarization gives $\langle u,v\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle\overline{\langle v,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle}\,dZ$, hence the weak resolution $$ u=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle g_Z^\epsilon\,dZ . $$

For $u\in\mathcal S$, the joint function $F(x,q):=u(x)e^{-|x-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}$ is Schwartz in $(x,q)$: each derivative is a finite sum of derivatives of $u$, Gaussian factors, and polynomials in $x-q$, and the inequality $\langle q\rangle^m\le C_m\langle x\rangle^m\langle x-q\rangle^m$ transfers every $q$-weight to a Schwartz factor and a Gaussian moment. Its partial Fourier transform in $x$ is Schwartz in $(p,q)$ by the same full Fourier/inverse Fourier argument as [F8]. The additional phase $e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}$ in $\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle$ has derivatives that are polynomial factors, so the packet coefficient $V_\epsilon u$ remains Schwartz in $Z=(q,p)$. The Schwartz seminorms of $Z\mapsto g_Z^\epsilon$ grow at most polynomially in $Z$, so the resolution integral in step 1.1 converges in every Schwartz seminorm. The product $u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz in $(x,y)$; its partial Fourier transform is Schwartz by [F8], so $\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\in\mathcal S$ and $|B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\le\|a\|_\infty\|\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\|_1$ proves continuity of the form in Schwartz seminorms. If $a\in\mathcal S$, its Weyl kernel is Schwartz; the kernel pairing is absolutely convergent, and the change $q=(x+y)/2,\ r=x-y$, followed by $r\mapsto-y$, identifies it with $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)$. Thus the bounded-symbol form extends the kernel definition on Schwartz symbols. Applying the continuous form to the two Schwartz-convergent resolutions is valid; Fubini [F5] for the resulting absolutely integrable products gives $$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\iint B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon)V_\epsilon u(Z')\overline{V_\epsilon v(Z)}\,dZ'\,dZ . $$

If $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$, its $L^1$ norm is $1$, hence $|B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq\|a\|_\infty$. If $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$, then $$ L_\delta:= rac{\epsilon}{i|\delta|^2}
abla_w\phi_\delta\cdot
abla_w,\qquad \phi_\delta(w):=-\sigma(w,\delta) $$ satisfies $L_\delta e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}=e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}$, since $|
abla_w\phi_\delta|=|\delta|$. Integrating by parts $N_d$ times against the Gaussian is justified coordinatewise by [F10] and Fubini [F5]: derivatives of the Gaussian are integrable, derivatives of $a$ are bounded, and the Gaussian forces the endpoint products to vanish. Translation $w=z-m$ and scaling $w=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$ in these absolutely integrable terms are justified by [F9]. Each derivative on the Gaussian contributes a factor bounded by $\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$; a derivative on $a$ contributes $\epsilon/|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$, since $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\leq1$. Increasing $C_d$ makes this bound valid also when $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$.

Partition $\mathbb R^{2d}$ into cubes of side $\sqrt\epsilon$. For each fixed $Z$, the sum of $(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}$ over these cubes, each weighted by its volume $\epsilon^d$, is at most $C_d\epsilon^d\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^{2d}}(1+|k|)^{-N_d}\leq C_d'\epsilon^d$, since $N_d=4d+4>2d$. These are rescaled versions of the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform; [F3], [F4], and the linear frequency scaling in [F8] imply they are Schwartz, integrable, and have inverse $a(z)=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int e^{i\lambda\cdot z}\widehat a(\lambda)\,d\lambda$. For $\lambda=(q,p)$, define the unitary map $$ (T^\epsilon_{q,p}u)(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p). $$ The phase has modulus one and [F6] preserves the norm under translation, so $T^\epsilon_{q,p}$ is unitary, with inverse given by reversing the translation and phase. Fourier inversion [F4], this formula, Fubini [F5], and [F8] applied to the complex $L^1$ integrands under $x\mapsto y=x+\epsilon p$ give the scalar form representation $$ \mathcal B_a(u,v):=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int\widehat a(\lambda)\langle T^\epsilon_\lambda u,v\rangle\,d\lambda . $$ For $u,v\in L^2$, this scalar integral is absolutely convergent and bounded by $(2\pi)^{-2d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$. For Schwartz $u,v$, use $T^\epsilon_{q,p}u(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p)$, change variables by [F8] to $y=x+\epsilon p$, and then apply Fourier inversion in $q$: $\int e^{iq\cdot(x+y)/2}\widehat a(q,(y-x)/\epsilon)\,dq=(2\pi)^d\int e^{-i(y-x)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a((x+y)/2,\xi)\,d\xi$. This gives $\mathcal B_a(u,v)=\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,v\rangle$. Both forms are bounded on $L^2\times L^2$, so [F7] extends their equality from the dense Schwartz subspace to all $L^2$ pairs; [F2] supplies the bounded Weyl extension.

Direct substitution in $T^\epsilon_{q,p}T^\epsilon_{q',p'}u$ gives the Weyl relation $$ T^\epsilon_\lambda T^\epsilon_\mu=e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}T^\epsilon_{\lambda+\mu}. $$ For $u,v\in L^2$, first apply [step 1.1] with $w=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u$; then $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u,v\rangle =(2\pi)^{-2d}\int\widehat a(\lambda)\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle\,d\lambda. $$ Apply [step 1.1] for $b$ to each pair $(u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v)$. Since $T_\lambda^\epsilon$ is unitary, $\langle T_\mu^\epsilon u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle=\langle T_\lambda^\epsilon T_\mu^\epsilon u,v\rangle$; the double integral is absolutely convergent with majorant $(2\pi)^{-4d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|\widehat b\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, so Fubini and the Weyl relation give $$ c_\epsilon(z)=(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,d\lambda\,d\mu . $$ The phase-space Fourier coefficient of $\{a,b\}$ is $-\sigma(\lambda,\mu)\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)$; this follows by differentiating the Fourier modes in the explicitly fixed Poisson convention.

Fix $\lambda,\mu$ and write $f(s)=e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}$, a $C^2$ complex function on $[0,1]$. Applying [F10] to the real and imaginary parts twice gives $f(1)-f(0)=\int_0^1f'(r)\,dr=f'(0)+\int_0^1\int_0^r f''(s)\,ds\,dr=f'(0)+\int_0^1(1-s)f''(s)\,ds$; the last equality is Fubini [F5] on the continuous integrand over the triangle. Since $f'(0)=-i\epsilon\sigma/2$ and $f''(s)=-\epsilon^2\sigma^2e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}/4$, this derives $$ e^{-i\epsilon\sigma/2}=1-\frac{i\epsilon\sigma}{2} -\frac{\epsilon^2\sigma^2}{4}\int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}\,ds. $$ Set $$ R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu):=\frac{\sigma(\lambda,\mu)^2}{4} \int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,ds . $$ Consequently the symbol remainder is $$ r_\epsilon(z)=-(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)\,d\lambda\,d\mu. $$ For multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ with $|\alpha|,|\beta|\le K:=4d+4$, differentiate $|\alpha|$ times in $z$ and integrate by parts $|\beta|$ times in $\lambda$ using [F9] coordinatewise to estimate $z^\beta\partial_z^\alpha r_\epsilon(z)$. Each integration is justified because the Fourier factors and all their derivatives have rapid decay and every differentiated factor has at most polynomial growth; thus the derivative products are integrable and boundary products vanish. Each $\lambda$-derivative of the remainder factor is bounded by $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)|\le C_\gamma\langle\lambda\rangle^2\langle\mu\rangle^{|\gamma|+2} \quad (|\gamma|\le K), $$ because $\sigma$ is bilinear, $\partial_\lambda\sigma$ is linear in $\mu$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$. Derivatives of $e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}$ contribute powers of $\lambda+\mu$. Thus the absolute integrand is bounded by a finite sum of $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma\widehat a(\lambda)|\,\langle\lambda\rangle^{K+2}\, |\widehat b(\mu)|\,\langle\mu\rangle^{2K+2}. $$ For completeness, in Fourier dimension $n=2d$, if $2k>L+n$, then $$ \int\langle\lambda\rangle^L|\partial^\gamma\widehat f(\lambda)|\,d\lambda \le C\sum_{|\delta|\le2k}\|\partial^\delta(z^\gamma f)\|_{L^1} \le C p_M(f) $$ whenever $M\ge2k$ and $M>|\gamma|+n$: apply $(1-\Delta_z)^k$ to $z^\gamma f$, use its Fourier multiplier $\langle\lambda\rangle^{2k}$, and integrate the resulting $\langle z\rangle^{-M+|\gamma|}$ bound. Taking $K=4d+4$, $L_a=K+2$, $L_b=2K+2$, choose $k_a=3d+4$ for $a$ and $k_b=5d+6$ for $b$. Then $2k_a>L_a+2d$, $2k_b>L_b+2d$, and $M=12d+16$ exceeds both $2k_b$ and $K+2d$, so the weighted estimates hold for all indicated derivatives. This proves $p_K(r_\epsilon)\le C_dp_M(a)p_M(b)$, uniformly in $\epsilon$. The same argument with any fixed larger $K$ proves every Schwartz seminorm of $r_\epsilon$ is finite, so $r_\epsilon\in\mathcal S$. Hence $c_\epsilon=ab+\frac{i\epsilon}{2}\{a,b\}+\epsilon^2r_\epsilon$ is Schwartz, and the weak Fourier representation from step 1.1 identifies the product in step 2.1 with $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(c_\epsilon)$.

The kernel of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_\epsilon)$, in $q=(x+y)/2$, $s=x-y$, is $$ K_\epsilon(q,s)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{is\cdot\xi/\epsilon}r_\epsilon(q,\xi)\,d\xi. $$ The affine map $(x,y)\mapsto(q,s)$ has absolute determinant $1$, and the kernel integrands are Schwartz and hence complex $L^1$, so [F8] justifies this kernel-coordinate substitution. Since $K=4d+4\ge2d+2$, $\langle(q,\xi)\rangle^K\ge\langle q\rangle^{d+1}\langle\xi\rangle^{d+1}$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\langle\xi\rangle^{-d-1}d\xi<\infty$ imply $\int|\partial_\xi^\gamma r_\epsilon(q,\xi)|\,d\xi\le C_dp_K(r_\epsilon)\langle q\rangle^{-d-1}$ for $|\gamma|\le2d+2$. Integrating by parts with $(1-\Delta_\xi)^{d+1}$ is justified coordinatewise by [F9], because $r_\epsilon$ is Schwartz; using this bound gives $$ |K_\epsilon(q,s)|\leq C_dp_{12d+16}(a)p_{12d+16}(b)\epsilon^{-d} \langle q\rangle^{-d-1}(1+|s|/\epsilon)^{-2d-2}. $$ For fixed $x$, $dy=2^d\,dq$ and $s=2(x-q)$; [F8] applies to these affine changes in the absolutely integrable row integrals, and integrating this bound in $y$ is at most a constant times $\epsilon^{-d}\int(1+|x-q|/\epsilon)^{-2d-2}\,dq\leq C_d$; the same bound holds with $x,y$ interchanged. Let $R$ and $C$ be the resulting uniform row and column $L^1$ bounds for the actual kernel $K_\epsilon(x,y)=K_\epsilon((x+y)/2,x-y)$. For $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$, Tonelli [F13] and the column bound make $\int|K_\epsilon(x,y)||u(y)|^2dy$ finite for almost every $x$. At such $x$, factor the integrand as $\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(x,y)|}\,[(K_\epsilon/|K_\epsilon|)(x,y)\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(x,y)|}u(y)]$, with quotient $0$ where the kernel vanishes. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] in $L^2(dy)$ gives $$ |\int K_\epsilon(x,y)u(y)\,dy|^2\le R\int|K_\epsilon(x,y)||u(y)|^2\,dy. $$ Tonelli [F13] and the column bound then give $\|\int K_\epsilon(\cdot,y)u(y)\,dy\|_2^2\le RC\|u\|_2^2$. This proves the integral-kernel Schur estimate with norm at most $\sqrt{RC}$ and hence $\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_\epsilon)\|\le C_dp_{12d+16}(a)p_{12d+16}(b)$. Combining steps 2.1–4.1 proves the asserted Weyl composition formula with the plus sign fixed by $[Q_j,P_k]=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $0<\epsilon\leq1$, and set $N_d=4d+4$. For a smooth $a:\mathbb R^{2d}\to\mathbb C$ with $\partial^\alpha a$ bounded for every $|\alpha|\leq N_d$, define

$$ \mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}\,dy $$

for $u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, and define the Weyl operator initially as the form

$$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v):=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi . $$

There is a unique bounded operator $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ representing this form, and

$$ \|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq C_d\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty , $$

where $C_d$ depends only on $d$. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, this extension agrees with the kernel definition in [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner].

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:

2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

$$ \frac{i}{\epsilon}[H_\epsilon^0,\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)] =\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(\{a,h\})+\epsilon^2\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a,V}). $$

$$ \sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha r_{\epsilon,a,V}\|_\infty \leq C_{d,V}p_{M_d}(a),\qquad p_M(f):=\max_{|\beta|\leq M}\sup_z\langle z\rangle^M|\partial^\beta f(z)|,\quad \langle z\rangle=(1+|z|^2)^{1/2}. $$

for $u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, and define the Weyl operator initially as the form

$$ \|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq C_d\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty , $$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$

derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

complex Hilbert space, let $Y$ be a dense linear subspace of $H$ that is itself
a Hilbert space continuously embedded in $H$ (for instance $Y=D(A_0)$ with the
graph norm of a self-adjoint $A_0$), let $T>0$, and let $A(t)$ for
$t\in[0,T]$ be an operator with $D(A(t))=Y$, self-adjoint as an operator on $H$,
such that $t\mapsto A(t)$ belongs to $C^1([0,T];\mathcal B(Y,H))$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Put $L:=\sup_t\|A'(t)\|_{\mathcal B(Y,H)}$.
Then:

(a) *Existence and uniqueness of a strong propagator.* There is a family
$U(t,s)$, $0\le s\le t\le T$, of unitary operators on $H$ with:
$U(s,s)=I$; $U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)$; $(t,s)\mapsto U(t,s)\xi$ continuous on
$\{s\le t\}$ for each $\xi\in H$; $U(t,s)Y=Y$ with
$\|U(t,s)y\|_Y\le C_T\|y\|_Y$ for a constant $C_T$ independent of
$(s,t)\in[0,T]^2$; and for every $y\in Y$ the map $t\mapsto U(t,s)y$ is $C^1$
in $H$ with
$$i\,\partial_tU(t,s)y=A(t)U(t,s)y,\qquad s\le t\le T.$$

(b) *Uniqueness.* If $V(t,s)$ is another family of bounded linear operators on $H$ with the same strong equation
on $Y$, $V(s,s)=I$ and $\sup_{r}\|V(r,s)y\|_{H}<\infty$, then $V=U$.

(c) *Equations for the reverse and adjoint.* $U(t,s)Y=Y$ for all $0\le s\le t\le T$
and $U(s,t):=U(t,s)^{-1}$ satisfies $i\partial_sU(s,t)y=A(s)U(s,t)y$ for
$y\in Y$; $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)$. Equivalently, differentiating the second
argument of the forward propagator gives $i\partial_sU(t,s)y=-U(t,s)A(s)y$.

obtained by $A=H_{\mathrm{energy}}/\hbar$ after choosing a time unit.

(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let $U_\epsilon(t)$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$; for $t<0$ it is the adjoint of the forward propagator at time $-t$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered by the first estimate. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference in that branch is identically zero.

There is also an exact statement for every real quadratic phase-space Hamiltonian. Let $z=(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, let $G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{2d\times2d}$, $\ell\in\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, and put
$$ h(z)=\tfrac12 z^TGz+\ell\cdot z+c. $$
Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_d\\-I_d&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\widehat z=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,P_1,\ldots,P_d)$, where $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. On $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ define the Weyl realization by
$$ H_{\epsilon,h}^0:=cI+\sum_j\ell_j\widehat z_j+\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}G_{jk}(\widehat z_j\widehat z_k+\widehat z_k\widehat z_j). $$
For each $0<\epsilon\le1$, assume a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_{\epsilon,h}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_{\epsilon,h}^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for it. Let $U_{\epsilon,h}(t)$ be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_{\epsilon,h}/\epsilon$. The global Hamiltonian flow, defined by $\dot z=J\nabla h(z)=J(Gz+\ell)$ and $\Phi_0(z)=z$, is
$$ \Phi_t(z)=e^{tJG}z+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)JG}J\ell\,ds. $$
Here $e^{tJG}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^n(JG)^n/n!$ is the matrix exponential.
Then for every $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$ U_{\epsilon,h}(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_{\epsilon,h}(t)=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t). $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite

The scaled oscillator eigenfunctions are polynomial multiples of $e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. To verify the core hypothesis of [[thm-nrqmx-quadratic-egorov]], take $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and set $L f=-\epsilon^2f''/2+x^2f/2\in L^2$. Integration by parts against each Hermite eigenfunction $\psi_n^\epsilon$, whose polynomial-Gaussian tails make the endpoint products vanish, gives
$ \langle Lf,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\langle f,L\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle. $
Parseval for the complete basis [F1] yields
$ \sum_{n\ge0}\epsilon^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle|^2 =\|Lf\|_2^2<\infty. $
Thus $f\in D(H_\epsilon)$. The coefficients of $H_\epsilon f$ in the Hermite basis are $\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle$, the same coefficients as $Lf$; completeness of that basis gives $H_\epsilon f=Lf$. The finite Hermite span is contained in $\mathcal S$ and is a graph core by [F1]; since $\mathcal S\subset D(H_\epsilon)$, $\mathcal S$ is also a core. This checks every operator hypothesis of [F4].

The Gaussian integral [F5] and the positive scaling in [F8] give $\|\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\|_2^2=(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}\int e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon}dx=1$. In its Wigner integral, the product of the two Gaussian factors is
$ (\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2}{\epsilon}-\frac{y^2}{4\epsilon}\right) \exp\!\left(\frac{ipy}{\epsilon}\right). $
Multiplying by $e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}$ and applying [F3] with $\eta=\xi-p$ gives
$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon} 2\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}\,e^{-(\xi-p)^2/\epsilon}, $
which is the stated nonnegative density. Its integral is $1$ by [F5] and [F8]. For its phase-space moments, apply [F8] to $x=q+\sqrt\epsilon s$ and $\xi=p+\sqrt\epsilon r$. The centered first moments vanish because $s e^{-s^2}$ and $r e^{-r^2}$ are odd; the cross-moment vanishes for the same reason. Integration by parts [F5] gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\frac12\int e^{-s^2}ds$, so each centered variance is $\epsilon/2$. This verifies the mean and covariance definitions in the Statement.
For the operator uncertainties, direct differentiation gives $P\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=\bigl(p+i(x-q)\bigr)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$, while $Q\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=x\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$. Thus $\bar Q_\psi=q$, $\bar P_\psi=p$, and the two squared standard deviations are both $\int(x-q)^2|\psi|^2dx=\epsilon/2$ by the same Gaussian integration by parts. To prove the lower bound for every normalized $\varphi\in\mathcal S$, first note that $Q$ and $P$ are symmetric on $\mathcal S$: for $P$ this is [F5] applied to decaying Schwartz factors, and for $Q$ it follows from real multiplication. Hence $\bar Q_\varphi,\bar P_\varphi\in\mathbb R$. Put $A=Q-\bar Q_\varphi I$ and $B=P-\bar P_\varphi I$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F6], the commutator $[A,B]=[Q,P]=i\epsilon I$ from [F2], and symmetry give
$ \Delta_\varphi Q\,\Delta_\varphi P\ge|\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|\ge|\operatorname{Im}\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|=\frac12|\langle[A,B]\varphi,\varphi\rangle|=\frac\epsilon2. $
Indeed, under the first-variable-linear convention, $\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle=\langle BA\varphi,\varphi\rangle$ and its conjugate is $\langle AB\varphi,\varphi\rangle$. Thus the Gaussian attains the lower bound.

The classical Hamilton equations for $h(x,\xi)=(x^2+\xi^2)/2$ solve to
$ \Phi_t(x,\xi)=(x\cos t+\xi\sin t,\ \xi\cos t-x\sin t). $
This matrix is orthogonal with determinant $1$, and $\Phi_t(q,p)=(q_t,p_t)$. For $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, [F4] gives
$ \langle W_t,a\rangle =\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}, \psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^2}a(\Phi_t z)W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](z)\,dz, $
where the last equality is [F2]. The integrand is in $L^1$ because $a$ is compactly supported and the Gaussian is integrable. Apply [F8] to the rotation $z'=\Phi_tz$; its determinant is $1$, so the resulting density is $W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](\Phi_{-t}z')$. Orthogonality gives
$ |\Phi_{-t}(x,\xi)-(q,p)|^2 =|(x,\xi)-\Phi_t(q,p)|^2, $
so this density is exactly the displayed $W_t$. The same change of variables sends its mean $(q,p)$ to $(q_t,p_t)$ and transforms covariance as $R_t(\epsilon I_2/2)R_t^T=\epsilon I_2/2$, since $R_t$ is orthogonal. This proves the asserted exact transport and covariance for every compactly supported smooth test symbol and hence for the distributional Wigner functional defined in the Statement.

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let $U_\epsilon(t)$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$; for $t<0$ it is the adjoint of the forward propagator at time $-t$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered by the first estimate. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference in that branch is identically zero.

There is also an exact statement for every real quadratic phase-space Hamiltonian. Let $z=(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, let $G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{2d\times2d}$, $\ell\in\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, and put
$$ h(z)=\tfrac12 z^TGz+\ell\cdot z+c. $$
Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_d\\-I_d&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\widehat z=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,P_1,\ldots,P_d)$, where $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. On $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ define the Weyl realization by
$$ H_{\epsilon,h}^0:=cI+\sum_j\ell_j\widehat z_j+\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}G_{jk}(\widehat z_j\widehat z_k+\widehat z_k\widehat z_j). $$
For each $0<\epsilon\le1$, assume a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_{\epsilon,h}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_{\epsilon,h}^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for it. Let $U_{\epsilon,h}(t)$ be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_{\epsilon,h}/\epsilon$. The global Hamiltonian flow, defined by $\dot z=J\nabla h(z)=J(Gz+\ell)$ and $\Phi_0(z)=z$, is
$$ \Phi_t(z)=e^{tJG}z+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)JG}J\ell\,ds. $$
Here $e^{tJG}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^n(JG)^n/n!$ is the matrix exponential.
Then for every $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$ U_{\epsilon,h}(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_{\epsilon,h}(t)=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t). $$

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. $$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1] and the oscillator scaling $\ell=\sqrt\epsilon$, the first excited state is $$ \ell^{-1/2}g_1(x/\ell) =\epsilon^{-1/4}\sqrt2\,\frac{x}{\sqrt\epsilon}\,\pi^{-1/4} e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)} =\sqrt{\frac2\epsilon}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4} x e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}. $$ The oscillator realization makes it a normalized Schwartz vector.

Write $A^2=2\epsilon^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}$. The product in the Wigner integrand is $$ \psi^\epsilon_1(x+y/2)\overline{\psi^\epsilon_1(x-y/2)} =A^2\left(x^2-\frac{y^2}{4}\right) e^{-x^2/\epsilon-y^2/(4\epsilon)}. $$ By [F4], $G_\epsilon''(\xi)=\int(-y^2/\epsilon^2)e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}dy$. Differentiating the explicit Gaussian in [F3] gives $$ \int y^2e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}dy =-\epsilon^2G_\epsilon''(\xi) =(2\epsilon-4\xi^2)G_\epsilon(\xi). $$ Substitution in the Wigner definition [F2] therefore yields $$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_1](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}A^2e^{-x^2/\epsilon} \left(x^2G_\epsilon(\xi)-\frac14(2\epsilon-4\xi^2)G_\epsilon(\xi)\right) =\frac1{\pi\epsilon} \left(\frac{2(x^2+\xi^2)}{\epsilon}-1\right) e^{-(x^2+\xi^2)/\epsilon}. $$ Every factor and sign follows from the displayed negative-sign Fourier convention.

The exponential and the prefactor $1/(\pi\epsilon)$ are strictly positive. Thus $W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_1](x,\xi)<0$ exactly when $2(x^2+\xi^2)/\epsilon-1<0$, which is the disk $x^2+\xi^2<\epsilon/2$. This normalized Schwartz vector refutes universal Wigner nonnegativity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
